fields.results: Analysis of the experimental data demonstrates that microgravity significantly stimulates sperm motility.  Furthermore, these results demonstrate a strong correlation between phosphorylation of flagellar phosphoproteins and sperm motility activation.  The aconeme-bound phosphoprotein FP130 (flagellar phosphoprotein) appeared to be the main target of changes in signal transduction pathways due to microgravity.  The temporal pattern of FP130 phosphorylation in microgravity is altered.  Because FP130 is also the target of speract (a chemotactic egg peptide), further study into the effect of microgravity on fertilization is necessary.

fields.approach: Twenty-one day old male spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR) were placed on either high calcium (2.0%) or low calcium (0.2%) diets. Indirect systolic blood pressure was measured at 5 and 7 weeks.  The 7 rats from the low calcium diet group with the highest blood pressure, as well as the 7 rats from the high calcium group with the lowest pressure, were selected for the flight portion of the experiment. They were placed in two animal enclosure modules (AEM), separated by diet, and flown on the 18 day STS-80 mission. After landing, indirect systolic blood pressure was measured. Then the rats were anesthetized and direct arterial blood pressure was determined with a catheter that was inserted into the carotid artery. The animal was exsanguinated and the mesenteric vascular bed was collected. First, normalized media thickness and lumen diameter were determined. Then the vessel segment was set to its initial length and media thickness and axial length were measured. Next, the normalized length was measured with the vessel stretched to 90% of the diameter that it would have with an intraluminal pressure of 100 mmHg. Each vessel was then subjected first to a challenge with 100 mmol/l KCl three times and then to a challenge with 100 mmol/l KCl plus 10 micromol/l norepinephrine twice and its contractile response was measured.

hardware.description:
The Ambient Temperature Recorder (ATR-4) is a self-contained, battery-powered instrument, approximately the size of a deck of cards. It may be placed in almost any environment (not submersible in liquid) to provide recording of up to four channels of temperature data. Channel 1 is selectable for either internal or external probe temperature sensing. Channels 2 through 4 are external only and require individual external temperature probes. External probes are flexible to allow the user to place probes at various locations within the sensed environment. Standard length for probes is three feet, but they may be longer or shorter, if required.

The temperature range is -40 °C to +60 °C. Data sample rate and number of channels are user-selectable. The total number of samples (32,400) is limited by the size of the ATR-4's solid state memory. When the memory is full, the recorder stops recording. Stored data may be read out postflight using a serial interface unit and an IBM-compatible computer. Power for the ATR-4 is provided by two internal batteries. An O-ring seal protects the ATR-4's internal electronics from fluids in the environment and permits operation in damp or humid environments such as an animal habitat.

fields.objectives: The inability of a vessel to increase resistance in the face of an orthostatic challenge is most likely associated with the problem of orthostatic intolerance. In animals that are exposed to simulated weightlessness, vascular contraction and regional blood flow is altered. The animal's ability to perform the necessary hemodynamic adjustments that are necessary to counter a sudden change in cardiac output may therefore be compromised.

payloads.description: Life sciences payloads on board STS-80 were the National Institutes of Health NIH.R4 and NIH.C6. NIH.R4 was designed to study the influence of dietary calcium and microgravity on calcium metabolism, blood pressure regulation, and vascular function. Beginning at three weeks of age and continuing throughout the experiment, a group of rats was maintained on either high or low calcium diets. At seven weeks of age, the two diet groups (n=7) were flown on the space shuttle Columbia Animal Enclosure Modules (AEMs) located in the Shuttle middeck. On recovery from the space shuttle and within six hours of landing, the rats' conscious blood pressure was measured; results showed that blood pressure was altered by both diet and microgravity. In particular, blood pressure was significantly higher in animals on low-calcium diets than animals on high-calcium diets, throughout the experiments. This adds to the body of knowledge necessary to maintaining the health of astronauts during space flight.

fields.results: Anesthetic conditions were found to be associated with differences in blood pressure between flight and control animals.  The flight groups' vascular contraction was found to be attenuated and relaxation to acetylcholine was diminished. However, there was no difference in relaxation due to sodium nitroprusside between the two groups.  Analysis suggests an alteration in endothelial function that may be associated with increased synthesis and release of nitric oxide. Overall, results point to the hypothesis that the problem of increasing vascular resistance in the mesenteric vascular bed is due to the animals' inability to divert blood flow from the viscera. Thus, decreased vessel responsiveness in visceral vascular beds may contribute to orthostatic intolerance.

fields.approach: The flight experiment consisted of six groups of ten neonates. The groups were housed in six nursing facilities that were contained within three Animal Enclosure Modules (AEM) and flown in shuttle middeck lockers. After landing, the P8 and P15 litters were studied for fourteen days. Swimming ability was measured daily by placing the animal in an aquarium and videotaping them for two minutes. Strokes that propelled the animal forward were counted and hindlimb angles were measured using the Peak5 Motion Measurement System. The free walking capabilities of the animals were also measured by videotaping their walking and analyzing their step cycle with the Peak System. Finally, surface righting ability was quantified using frame by frame analysis.

fields.objectives: This study makes use of neonatal mammals in order to study the effects of microgravity on the development of the nervous system. Altering gravity during development provides a noninvasive technique by which the influence of motor activity on the development of the nervous system may be studied. Neonates offer a unique and valuable model for experimentation because they possess critical periods of development during which an organism's development is most sensitive to environmental changes.

payloads.description: STS-72 included two life sciences payloads—NIH.R3 and NIH.C5—both collaborations between NASA and the National Institutes of Health. NIH.R3 demonstrated the Animal Enclosure Module (AEM) nursing facility, a modified Animal Enclosure Module System designed to support nursing rats and neonates. Validating the suitability of sending lactating female rats and neonates into space is important because they have not flown in space before and are essential for studying the effects of microgravity on early development.

fields.approach: The hFOB 1.19 was used, which is a conditionally immortalized line that expresses the mature osteoblastic phenotype.   Standard conditions were used to culture the hFOB cell line, except that they were incubated at 37 degrees C, instead of at 34 degrees C. For each experimental cartridge, cells were attached by gently mixing 600,000 cells with 50 mg of Cytodex beads and incubating them for 45 minutes in 15 ml conical tubes with 5 ml of equilibrated DME/F12+10%FBS+G418 at 37 degrees C. The cartridges were then inserted into the CCM and incubated for 2 days prior to launch. 4 ml fractions were collected on days 1, 4, 8, and 12 from both flight cultures and ground control cultures. After recovery, the ends of the cartridges were cut and hollow fiber bundles were removed. The cells, beads, and collagenous matrix was scraped into 1X PBS, and RNA was isolated using the method of Chomczynski. After ethanol precipitation, RNA pellets were quantitated using UV spectrophotometry for Northern or RNase protection assays. For the Northern assays, total RNA isolated was denatured, separated by agarose gel electrophoresis, and bound to nylon filter by vacuum baking. After being hybridized, blots were exposed to phosphoimager screens. With a Molecular Dynamics Phosphoimager, band intensities were quantitated. In the RNase protection assay, RNA was hybridized, treated, separated by gel electrophoresis, and vacuum dried. Band intensities were quantitated on a phosphoimager screen. Procollagen was quantitated in a gamma counter and was then compared to a standard curve of known PICP standards. Enzyme immunoassay was used to measure the level of prostaglandin E2 in the hFOB conditioned media. A small sample of cells and beads was fixed for electron microscopy.

components.description: The STL-A has space for four separate experiments, each one housed in a separate module or Bioreactor Rail Assembly. The Bioreactor Rail Assembly holds a variable number of bioreactor cartridges. These cartridges, which are inlaid with hollow fibers, provide an exchange surface for nutrient media and gas, as well as a site for removal of waste products. Hollow-fiber bioreactors can also be used to grow cultures in three dimensions. For culturing larger pieces of tissue, fiberless cartridges are available.

components.description:
Nutrients and gas are provided to the cells via a closed-loop flow that can be delivered in either a recirculating or intermittent flow.

The recirculating flow path option directs media flow through a media bag, oxygenator, pump, biochamber, then back to the media bag. This allows growth factors and other products to accumulate.

A second option, the intermittent feed, periodically pumps fresh media into a short flow path that recirculates in the same manner as the first option, but is eventually diverted to a sump and replaced with fresh media.

The system offers a variety of biological sample maintenance systems, variable temperature settings, options for media delivery and collection of conditioned media samples, and programmed additions of drugs, hormones, radioactive labels, and other experiment requirements.

The STL-A contained four Bioreactor Rail Assemblies loaded with polypropylene fiber cartridges. During flight, the cartridges were maintained at an incubation temperature of approximately 37 °C and media was delivered by both the recirculating and intermittent feed methods.

NIH.C2, NIH.C5, and NIH.C7 Configurations:

The module included custom Bioreactor Rail Assemblies and custom heat sinks in order to accommodate the bio-artificial muscle preparation required for the experiment 9304010. fields.objectives: It has long been known that microgravity has a degenerative effect upon bone cell formation. Previous research suggests that bone loss is due to a decrease in bone cell formation. Therefore, this study focuses on the response of osteoblast to both microgravity and a return to Earth. Gene expression, matrix production, and cell function were monitored during the 17 day mission and after landing.

payloads.description: Life sciences payloads on board STS-80 were the National Institutes of Health NIH.R4 and NIH.C6. NIH.C6 (renamed to CCM-A) continued the investigation into how microgravity affects bones at the cellular level. To examine the response of bone-forming cells to weightlessness, human fetal osteoblastic (hFOB) cells were cultured then analyzed for glucose utilization, type I collagen and prostaglandin E2 accumulation, and gene expression for several bone matrix proteins. The results suggest that space flight does not significantly affect these variables.

fields.results: Results suggest that hFOB cells responded to space flight primarily in cytokine gene expression rather than in cell function and proliferation. It is especially notable that hFOB cells showed vigorous growth during flight. Gene expression, glucose utilization, and PGE2 and type I collagen accumulation were not significantly affected by prolonged exposure to microgravity. In microgravity, both type I collagen accumulation and PGE2 accumulations were unaffected. Flight and ground control cells showed no qualitative difference in morphology. These results suggest that hFOB cells may have a reduced response to microgravity in relation to rat bone cells. Further analysis suggests that dynamic loading is the dominant factor in regulating bone mass over static loading.

fields.approach: Flight rats and ground control rats were 26 days old at the beginning of the experiment.  Rats were flown for 5.4 days and muscles were removed within 3 hours of landing. Body weights and muscle weights were measured for flight and control rats. Protein analysis for total protein content and concentration was performed on the soleus, gastrocnemius, plantaris, tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum. The soleus and extensor digitorum were used for glucose uptake studies. The extensor digitorum served as a control to the soleus because it is not affected by loading or systemic effects. The uptake of 2-deoxyglucose was measured in the presence and absence of insulin.

hardware.description:
The Ambient Temperature Recorder (ATR-4) is a self-contained, battery-powered instrument, approximately the size of a deck of cards. It may be placed in almost any environment (not submersible in liquid) to provide recording of up to four channels of temperature data. Channel 1 is selectable for either internal or external probe temperature sensing. Channels 2 through 4 are external only and require individual external temperature probes. External probes are flexible to allow the user to place probes at various locations within the sensed environment. Standard length for probes is three feet, but they may be longer or shorter, if required.

The temperature range is -40 °C to +60 °C. Data sample rate and number of channels are user-selectable. The total number of samples (32,400) is limited by the size of the ATR-4's solid state memory. When the memory is full, the recorder stops recording. Stored data may be read out postflight using a serial interface unit and an IBM-compatible computer. Power for the ATR-4 is provided by two internal batteries. An O-ring seal protects the ATR-4's internal electronics from fluids in the environment and permits operation in damp or humid environments such as an animal habitat.

fields.objectives:
Data originated from Marc Tischler's NASA grant "Physiological and Anatomical Rodent Experiment 1."

Previous to PARE 01, the only studies comparing unweighting through microgravity and unweighting through hindlimb suspension were performed on adult rats. These studies have shown that posterior hindlimb muscles, the function of which depend on opposing the pull of gravity, are the most responsive to unweighting. Another effect found in unweighting studies has been the increased response of insulin to glucose transport. This experiment was designed to test the validity of using tail suspension methods as models for studying microgravity unweighting effects on developing rats. Several muscle parameters were compared between rats subjected to space flight and rats subjected to hindlimb suspension. A main objective was to determine whether microgravity causes an increase in glucose uptake in the presence or absence of insulin.

payloads.description: The life sciences payload on this mission was called the Physiological and Anatomical Rodent Experiment-01 (PARE.01). This experiment was designed to study muscle atrophy, glucose transport, and metabolism in microgravity. A ground-based tail-suspension model was also studied during this experiment to determine whether microgravity could be effectively simulated on Earth for the purpose of studying space flight-induced muscle atrophy.

fields.results: Despite similar food and water consumption, flight rats gained more weight than the control rats. Comparisons of muscle sizes normalized to body mass showed that flight and suspension reduced muscle mass of the soleus by 38 percent and 33 percent respectively. Smaller differences were seen in masses of plantaris and gastrocnemius muscles and no differences were seen in anterior muscles. Protein content of the soleus muscles from flight rats was reduced by 20 percent and was characterized by a lower concentration. Protein content from the soleus muscles of suspended rats was reduced by 23 percent. In the absence of insulin, there was no difference in the rate of uptake of 2-deoxyglucose in the soleus or the extensor digitorum. However, in the presence of insulin, the uptake of 2-deoxyglucose was significantly higher in flight and suspended rats than in control rats. This increase may be due to an increase in insulin binding capacity due to unloading effects.

fields.approach:
Cells, suspended in medium containing 2% fetal calf serum, are held at ambient temperature (20oC) for approximately twenty hours until activation of the experiment in microgravity.  After the samples are incubated at 37°C for 1 hour, they are brought to the Biorack glovebox for growth activation by increasing the serum concentration to 10%.  One sample set is placed in the 1g in-flight centrifuge; the other is held static.  Both sets are incubated at 37oC for varying periods of time after which they are fixed with formalin or an RNA stabilizing solution.

Membrane-cytoskeletal interactions are involved in second messenger transduction by a signal amplification mechanism and intact microtubules are required: therefore, several specific scientific aims are defined to address the different steps of this complex process.

1) Evaluate the effects of spaceflight on the gross morphology of the cytoskeleton in human T cells (Jurkat).

2) Assess early signal transduction in growth-stimulated lymphocytes by evaluating protein kinase C (PKC) translocation in cells (an immediate response after mitogen binding and growth stimulation) and PKC gene expression after 24 hours.  Cells from spaceflight are evaluated for PKC mRNA to determine if this gene is up-or down-regulated compared to the ground and in-flight 1-g control samples.

3) Investigate the turnover of inositol phosphate (IP, PIP2, IP3) at the cell membrane to evaluate very early signal transduction. (To be done if peripheral blood lymphocytes are flown).

4) Evaluate expression of selected cytoskeleton-associated genes including genes that encode for actin, tubulin, and the regulatory proteins, gelsolin and profilin since these cytoskeleton-associated proteins are involved in signal transduction.  

5) To investigate the relationship and/or requirements for dendritic cells to facilitate lymphocyte activation in low gravity. The blunted response of lymphocytes in space may be a result of reduced secretion of interleukin-1 (IL-1) by monocytes.  However, the influence of accessory cells(dendritics) has not been addressed.  (This objective will only be met if hardward units and crew time are available to fly peripheral blood lymphocytes in addition to Jurkat cells). 

6)  To understand or rule-out stress s as a reason for failure of T cell populations to increase in number in micrograivty, mRNA for heat-shock proteins is evaluated by RT-PCR (Reverse Transcriptase - Polymerase Chain Reaction).  

7)  To determine if programmed cell death (apoptosis) is a factor in lympyhocyte population growth arrest during spaceflight, the percentage of cells showing nuclear apoptotic bodies are determined and nitric oxide (NO) levels in culture medium may be measured.  

8)  To address T lymphocyte responsiveness to growth stimulation, levels of secreted lympholines (IL-1ß, IL-2, TNF-alpha and gamma interferon) are monitored using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA).  (This aim depends on whether crew time and hardware is available to fly peripheral blood lymphocytes).

hardware.description: The time between the loading of biological samples into the Shuttle and the activation of the experiment by the crew requires special equipment to maintain certain temperatures. Passive Thermal Conditioning Units (PTCUs) are storage containers for Biorack experiments, which fit into a middeck locker and can maintain a predetermined temperature over a twelve-day period. The PTCUs harness the latent heat capacity at the melting point of selected waxes and insulate the wax from the warm environment by double, stainless steel Dewar vessels. To improve thermal insulation before the samples are loaded, the volume between the double walls of the Dewar vessels is increased by vacuum pump up to 10-9 Torr. The vessels are also heated to 130°C to remove any water vapor. A rack for 16 Biorack Type I and one Type II experiment containers, or 20 Type I containers alone, can fit inside a PTCU. The PTCUs fit into an aluminum case called the Middeck Locker Stowage Insert (MLSI).

components.description:
Each ATCU contains a cooler/freezer, incubators, and a glovebox.

Cooler/Freezer
The cooler/freezer is a combined unit that allows the maintenance of biological samples at temperatures that inhibit their metabolism. The cooler is capable of maintaining samples just above the freezing point (4 degrees Celsius). The freezer section can conserve samples at temperatures as low as -15 °C.

Incubators
The ATCU has two incubators that can be set accurately between 18 and 40 °C. Two centrifuges are included in each incubator to simulate a 1-g environment. Control samples, identical to those being exposed to microgravity conditions, are placed in these centrifuges. Comparing these two sets of samples, after their processing in the incubator has finished, permits the microgravity and radiation-environment effects to be identified.

Glovebox
The glovebox is a small working area for handling and observing biological specimens. The observations can be made through a microscope that is connected to photo, film, or TV cameras.

Experiment hardware must fit in one of two types of sealed, anodized aluminum containers. Type I containers measure 90x58x24 mm, and Type II containers measure 79x79x99 mm. Each type of container can be connected electrically to the Biorack and are thus named Type I/E and Type II/E. Likewise, non-electrified containers are named Type I/O and Type II/O.

hardware.description:
Biorack is a reusable, multi-user facility developed by the European Space Agency (ESA) for studying the effects of microgravity and radiation on cellular functions and developmental processes in plants, tissues, cells, bacteria, and small invertebrates. The facility is equipped with a cooler/freezer, two incubators, and a glovebox. Experiment hardware must fit in one of two types of sealed, anodized aluminum containers. Type I containers are 90x58x24 mm and Type II containers are 79x79x99 mm.

The main parts of the Biorack are the Active Thermally Controlled Units (ATCUs), the Passive Thermal Conditioning Units (PTCUs), Stowage, and Aluminum Containers.

hardware.versionDescription:
The Biorack on IML-1 flew with one cooler/freezer; two incubators; a glovebox; stowage; aluminum containers for experiment-specific hardware; and five PTCUs: one at 10 °C, three at 5 °C, and one at -10 °C.

US-3 (IML-1) Configuration:
The experiment also had its own supplementary hardware which was stored in Biorack Type I aluminum containers within the Biorack facility.

US-3 Cell Chambers: Limb bud cell cultures were contained in a Lexan polycarbonate chamber with two wells. Each well had a "bubble" of a gas-changing material, which expanded or collapsed as medium was added or removed. A silicon rubber gasket and bottom plate completed the basic assembly. Cells were cultured on coverslips inserted between the gasket and bottom plate. A deflector ring in the bottom of the chamber prevented fluid forces—produced during the medium injection and withdrawal—from dislodging or shearing the cells on the coverslip.

US-3 Chamber Assemblies: Four culture chambers (eight chamber wells) were inverted and placed on a tray designed to fit into a Type I container, thus allowing the four culture chambers to be removed as a unit. The chamber units were held in place in the tray by double-sided, sticky-backed tape. The medium exchange and fixation were performed by inserting a hypodermic needle through the gasket and onto the cultures on the cover slip.

Syringe Racks: The syringe racks held the syringes used to perform medium exchange and fixation of the cell cultures. The racks, made of Lexan polycarbonate, were designed in three different arrangements such that each one fit into a different location: the middeck locker stowage insert, the cooler, or the freezer. The cooler rack held 40 syringes filled with replacement medium. The stowage rack held the replacement-medium syringes that were transferred from the cooler rack following the Biorack's activation. Finally, the freezer rack stored syringes that contain removed, conditioned medium.

US-3 (STS-76) Configuration:
Biorack on STS-76 contained two incubators and a glovebox, but no active cooling device. One incubator was maintained at 22 °C and the other at 36.5 °C. The incubators each contained new, variable-speed centrifuges, different from those that flew on IML-1. The new centrifuges were equipped with brushless d.c. motors and new control electronics. They could run at any one of three, pre-set, rotational speeds, resulting in three different levels of acceleration force.

The Biorack also contained three PTCUs: two at 5 °C and one at -10 °C.

The experiment also had its own supplementary hardware which was stored in Biorack Type I aluminum containers within the Biorack facility.

US-3 Cell Activation Kit-1 (Cytokines): The kit consists of polycarbonate blocks or "cassettes," each stored in a Type I container. Each cassette is made up of six independent culture chambers and associated daughter chambers. The chambers can be manipulated by turning vanes to connect or to isolate them from each other or by pushing pistons to displace fluid from chamber to chamber. Activators can be added and supernatant filtered from cells by means of a filtering system within the cassette. After filtration, cells can be resuspended into the cassette using a multi-injector unit.

fields.objectives: Data from 20 years of manned spaceflight consistently show reduced response of human T lymphocytes to mitogen-induced (mitogenic) challenge during and for several days after flight.  Cells in vitro are also resistant to mitogen stimulation. Reasons are unclear.  The objective of the study is to investigate the role of the cytoskeleton in gravity (microgravity) "sensing" and signal transduction in single cells (lymphocytes) using the human T lymphocyte cell line (Jurkat) and peripheral blood lymphocytes if crew time and hardware space is available.  Specific aims are to evaluate 1) cytoskeletal morphology; 2) signal transduction mechanisms; and 3) expression of genes regulating cytoskeletal and related proteins. Membrane-cytoskeleton interactions leading to signal transduction and growth response require an intact cytoskeleton.  New information on mechanisms relating the cytoskeleton to blunted human T cell responsiveness, thus immunity, during spaceflight is applicable to both space- and Earth-based medicine. This information may facilitate drug design and countermeasure development and may have ramifications for the treatment of cancer (Jurkat is a cell line derived from from acute human T-cell leukemia). The main objective of the experiment is to contribute to the database on the effect of spaceflight on single cells.  Molecular and gene-level responses are studied in an attempt to explain depressed T lymphocyte growth activation during spaceflight compared to normal Earth-gravity and the 1g in-flight centrifuge controls.

payloads.description:
The Biorack experiments studied the effects of microgravity and cosmic radiation, particularly the effects of high-energy particles on the development of plants, tissues, cells, bacteria and insects during spaceflight.  Developed by the European Space Agency (ESA), the Biorack is a complete experiment rack that fits into the Spacehab module. It consists of two incubators with 1- g reference centrifuges, a glovebox, and a refrigerator/freezer unit.  Among the international set of Biorack investigations were a study of microgravity on bone loss, the effects of using centrifuges as 1-g references for the microgravity tests; cell response, repair, activation, and gene expression in microgravity; developmental processes; plant experiments; and a dosimetry experiment to document the radiation environment inside the Biorack facility and other locations inside the SPACEHAB module and middeck.

The three U.S. investigations were as follows:

BIORACK: Microgravity Effects on Bone Cell Gene Expression (OSTEO)
BIORACK: Mechanisms of Gravity Sensing and Response in Hematopoietic Cells (TCELL)
BIORACK: Modification of Radiogenic Damage By Microgravity (ELEGANS)

fields.results:
Spaceflown Jurkat cells were metabolically active (using approximately 1.6 times more glucose at 48 hours than the ground controls in both static (P = 0.0046) and centrifuged (P = 0.0003) cultures) (PARAM 002986) but cells did not grow in microgravity (PARAM 002985). By comparison, ground control cells almost doubled within the same 48 hrs (hours). Because flown cells did not proliferate, the possibility of cell cycle arrest was evaluated by flow cytometry. Flown cells showed initial  arrest in G2M (both static microgravity and 1g in-flight controls) at 4 hours. By 48 hrs, no significant differences in cell cycle distribution were found and cells appeared to be distributed across all cell cycle phases (PARAM 002987).

The following results were obtained for each Scientific aim listed above:

1) Cytoskeletal morphology: (PARAM 000738) Microtubule organizing centers (MTOC) were poorly organized in flown cells fixed at 4 hrs compared to ground controls. Microtubules appeared as randomly oriented, thickened cables of shortened filaments that terminated before reaching the cell membrane. These elements appeared to reorganize in flight by 48 hrs. 

Though not an original aim, the effect of simulated shuttle launch vibration on microtubule morphology was evaluated (as ground-based test).  Duplicate samples of vibrated and non-vibrated cells were fixed with formalin at 10 minutes, and 4, 24 and 48 hrs after vibration. 
In cells fixed at 10 minutes and 4 hrs after vibration the microtubules appeared coalesced, randomly distributed, and prematurely terminated (similar to flown cells). Many small, brightly stained dots, assumed to be depolymerized tubulin or disorganized MTOCs were observed.  By 24 hrs, the microtubule cytoskeleton appeared to be re-established, and at 48 hrs cytoskeletal staining at the focal contacts between cells was restored. Vibration stress did not up-regulate the cell death factor, Fas/APO-1, nor increase glucose utilization as seen in the flown cells (see below).

2) Early Signal transduction: (PARAM 000975) This aim was achieved through collaboration with Co-Investigators (Didier Schmitt and Jason Hatton). The experiment was flown on a different Biorack payload using peripheral blood lymphocytes and U937 cells. Protein Kinase C (PKC) translocation from the cytosol to the nucleus, membrane, and insoluble cytoskeleton occurred in cells in microgravity, the in-flight 1g control, and ground and 1.4g  controls.  Differences in translocation for several isoforms were related to T cell storage before activation in microgravity.

3, 5 & 8) IP3 trunover (PARAM 001803), Dendritic cells, Secreted lymphokines (PARAM 001898): These parameters would have been investigated if peripheral blood lymphocytes could have been flown in the TCELL experiment on STS-76. Due to the hardware availability and crew time limitations, experiments using peripheral blood lymphocytes were not flown and these objectives could not be achieved.

4) Cytoskeletal gene expression (PARAM 001183, PARAM 001381, PARAM 001553), PARAM 001553, PARAM 002988): Gene expression analyses planned for the STS-76 Biorack flight were not achieved because of a technical problem in preserving RNA message.  However, this objective was accomplished by use of residual Jurkat cells flown on STS-95 on a different payload.  STS-76 Biorack funding was used to analyze gene expression by cDNA microarray and, for some genes, by RT-PCR.  More than 4,324 genes (at 24 hrs) and 20,000 genes (at 48 hours) were evaluated by cDNA microarray in flown versus ground controls. (This is the first experiment to evaluate expression of thousands [>20,000]of genes by cDNA microarray in human lymphocytes). Though not a primary aim of the original Biorack proposal, Jurkat cells were also subjected to simulated shuttle launch vibration as a control to determine effect of vibration on gene expression.  More than 4,324 genes were evaluated in vibrated cells at 4, 24, and 48 hrs. (The following URL address permits direct access to 53 pages of tabulated gene expression data for flown and vibrated cells:  http://www.fasebj.org/cgi/content/abstract/00-
0820fjev1?ijkey=4kpP6Xbf7y/0o&keytype=ref&siteid=fasebj)
Expression levels of 10 cytoskeleton-related genes were up-regulated in space-flown compared to ground control cells (calponin, dynactin, tropomodulin, keratin 8, two myosins, an ankyrin EST, an actin-like protein, the cytoskeletal linker (plectin) and a centriole-associated protein (C-NAP1)). A gelsolin precursor gene (PARAM 001553) was down-regulated. Message for actin (PARAM 001183), tubulin (PARAM 001381) profilin (PARAM 001695), and PKC-related genes was unchanged. Up-regulation of plectin and C-NAP1 message in both spaceflown and vibrated cells is a novel finding and implies their role in vibration damage repair. Differential expression of genes that regulate growth, metabolism, signal transduction, adhesion, transcription, apoptosis, and tumor suppression was identified.   
From these data we conclude that centriole-centriole, membrane-cytoskeletal, and cytoskeletal filament associations are altered in microgravity. Up-regulation in spaceflown cells of plectin, dynactin, C-NAP1, and tropomodulin and down-regulation of gelsolin precursor genes is of particular interest since these proteins are mediators of cytoskeletal organization.

6) Evaluation of Heat Shock proteins (PARAM 002988): Spaceflight did not up-regulate mRNA levels for Heat Shock Protein (HSP) 70. The gene encoding HSP27 was up-regulated by spaceflight but not by ground-based simulated launch vibration. Up-regulation of HSP27 gene expression in microgravity is a new finding. In ground controls, the mRNA for HSP70 and HSP27 increased with cell density and time in culture. HSP70 gene expression is a useful indicator of stress related to culture density but does not appear to be an indicator of launch vibration stress or microgravity. 

7) Apoptosis: (PARAM 000227) A significantly higher number of apoptotic cells was found in cells fixed in microgravity at 4 hrs. Centrifugation (1g in space and 1.4g ground control) increased the number of apoptotic cells compared to non-centrifuged cultures. Identification of the time-dependent, microgravity-related cell death (apoptosis) factor (Fas/APO-1) suggests this as a possible mechanism mediating lymphocyte population dynamics during spaceflight.

fields.approach: Prior to flight, rats received injections of either MK-217 or a vehicle control. All rats received injections of the bone marker calcein.  Post-flight, all rats received injections of a second bone marker, oxytetracycline. Urine, blood, fecal and oropharyngeal samples were taken. The animals were then euthanized and immediately shipped to the commercial partner's laboratory for further analysis of the effects of microgravity and the proprietary compound on cortical bone formation and resorption.

hardware.description:
The Ambient Temperature Recorder (ATR-4) is a self-contained, battery-powered instrument, approximately the size of a deck of cards. It may be placed in almost any environment (not submersible in liquid) to provide recording of up to four channels of temperature data. Channel 1 is selectable for either internal or external probe temperature sensing. Channels 2 through 4 are external only and require individual external temperature probes. External probes are flexible to allow the user to place probes at various locations within the sensed environment. Standard length for probes is three feet, but they may be longer or shorter, if required.

The temperature range is -40 °C to +60 °C. Data sample rate and number of channels are user-selectable. The total number of samples (32,400) is limited by the size of the ATR-4's solid state memory. When the memory is full, the recorder stops recording. Stored data may be read out postflight using a serial interface unit and an IBM-compatible computer. Power for the ATR-4 is provided by two internal batteries. An O-ring seal protects the ATR-4's internal electronics from fluids in the environment and permits operation in damp or humid environments such as an animal habitat.
hardware.name: Ambient Temperature Recorder (ATR-4)

hardware.versionDescription: The ATR-4 was flown on Shuttle missions as described.

fields.objectives: Degenerative changes observed in the musculoskeletal systems of both astronauts and animals during prolonged exposure to weightlessness parallel the slower changes in bone and muscle mass seen during the aging process on Earth. This experiment aims to use this similarity to test the effectiveness of a Merck & Co. proprietary compound (MK-217) in preventing bone loss, for possible future use in treating disuse osteoporosis. The morphological and physiological effects of MK-217 on bone formation and resorption during a nine day spaceflight were measured.  The experiment also used the data collected to analyze the effectiveness of the bone unloading experienced during microgravity exposure as a model for disuse osteoporosis.

payloads.description: Life sciences payloads on this mission included the Physiological Systems Experiment-02 (PSE.02), a proprietary experiment developed by Merck & Co., Inc. and the Center for Cell Research, a NASA Center for the Commercial Development of Space located at Pennsylvania State University. PSE.02 used the premise that microgravity and osteoporosis have the same effect on bone to test a compound designed to slow or halt bone loss.

After sacrifice, the sponges were removed and prepared for biochemical and histological analysis of DNA, protein, and collagen content. Histological organization, amount of visible collagen, and the resolution of hemorrhage at the infiltrating interface were also examined.

fields.objectives: Little is currently known about the effects of microgravity on tissue repair. In the era of a long-term human presence in space, the probability of minor injury requiring on orbit treatment will increase. This experiment aims to evaluate the effects of spaceflight on the histological and tensiometric properties of full-thickness abdominal incisional skin wounds in the rat. A second objective was to evaluate the effectiveness of basic fibroblast growth factor (FGF) and platelet-derived growth factor (bb-homodimer, PDGF) in promoting granulation tissue formation and collagen deposition.

payloads.description: The life sciences payload on STS-57 was a proprietary experiment developed by ConvaTec, a Bristol-Myers Squibb Company; and the Center for Cell Research, a NASA Center for the Commercial Development of Space located at Pennsylvania State University. The experiment, Physiological Systems Experiment.03 (PSE.03), investigated the roles of two growth factors in accelerating or enhancing tissue repair.  Such information would be useful for designing therapies for astronauts who incur skin or soft-tissue injuries during prolonged space flight.

fields.results: Histological analysis showed that both bFGF and PDGF showed positive effects in the ground control rats, but only immediate-release bFGF and delayed-release PDGF had significant, positive effects in the flight rats. This may be due to the 2-day launch delay of the shuttle mission, which caused the growth factor to be released earlier during flight than planned. Although cellular influx into the tissue space of placebo-treated sponges was unaffected by spaceflight, there was a significantly blunted response to either bFGF or PDGF-BB in flight animals. Microgravity significantly reduced wound collagen concentration regardless of the treatment group. The collagen concentration of granulation tissue in flight animals treated with bFGF was significantly less than in those treated with PDGF, but not significantly less than in the placebo treated group. These results show that a highly standardized wound repair process in young rats is significantly altered by spaceflight.

fields.approach: Primate selection and training began 2.5 years prior to flight at the Institute of Medical Primatology colony. The original pool was reduced from 100 to 25 monkeys. Those animals underwent tail removal surgery, and were then transferred to the Institute of Biomedical Problems (IMBP) in Moscow. In July of 1995, 12 monkeys were selected for surgical implantation of electrodes and cannulas, and underwent muscle and bone biopsies. In September of 1996, flight-type experiments were initiated. Animals experiencing difficulty with the implants were either culled from the pool or used in control experiments. Animals #357 and #484 were selected as prime crew, and #513, #501, #477, and #534 were selected as backups. The selected animals were transported to the cosmodrome Plesetsk in late November 1996.

payloads.description:
Mission Overview

Bion 11 was the payload that flew on the Cosmos biosatellite mission of 1996. The payload was a collaborative endeavor pursued by the American, Russian, and French space agencies. Its 14-day mission began on December 24, 1996 with the launch of the Vostok space capsule from the Plesetsk cosmodrome in Russia. The capsule carried two rhesus monkeys as well as other life sciences and microgravity experiments.

Bion 11 was intended to define qualitatively and quantitatively the effect of weightlessness on primate physiology and the mechanisms underlying those changes. Fields of investigation included the effects of weightlessness on bone, muscle and neuromuscular structure and function; sensorimotor function; behavior; circadian rhythms; fluid and electrolyte balance; and immunology.  Also studied was the way that the body readapts to normal gravity following landing.

Other Bion 11 experiments included a study of how a number of different organisms  respond physiologically to microgravity, including Dileptus anfer (a protist) Pottia and Caretodou mosses on agar, Lepidium savita L. seedlings on a solid substrate, fruit flies, black body beetles, and Spanish newts. Radiation experiments on dry seeds, nucleotides and bacterial spores were also conducted.

The Bion 11 flight was successfully completed when the spacecraft landed in Kazakhstan on January 7, 1997. One of the monkeys died during anesthesia induction for its post-landing medical operation and check-up, which occurred shortly after its capsule was recovered. This incident raised questions with respect to the use of anesthesia on astronauts post flight, and results of the investigation potentially saved the lives of future astronauts.  The Bion 11 and 12 investigations were supposed to have been a two-mission series with major objectives aimed at understanding the source of muscle and bone weakening in space; however, the monkey's death compromised certain of these studies.

fields.approach: Muscle biopsies were taken from flight, capsule control, and vivarium control monkeys approximately 100 days before launch and at R+1. Samples were frozen, and cut into serial cross-sections 10 _m thick. Sections were pre-incubated at pH 4.2 and stained for succinate dehydrogenase (both muscles) or myofibrillar ATPase (m. soleus only). Cross-sectional areas (CSA) of types I and type II fibers were measured from each biopsy. Morphometric measurements were made in a minimum of 50 fibers of each type. In the m. vastus lateralis, total protein, mitochondrial respiration, mitochondrial creatine kinase, oxygen uptake, and mitochondrial respiration were measured. After measurements were made, muscle fibers were dried and weighed. In the m. soleus,  capillary/fiber ratio, capillary density, and total protein were measured.

fields.objectives: Changes in the structure and metabolism of the skeletal muscles of the leg have been observed in both humans and animals after space flight. Some examples of the effects of microgravity on skeletal muscle are changes in the cross-sectional area of slow- and fast-twitch muscle fibers, decreases in fiber size (muscle atrophy), and decreases in oxidative potential and number of capillaries. Although most investigators believe that the major factor affecting these changes in the extensor muscles is the gravitational unloading experienced in space, others believe that factors such as physical exercise or dehydration may also have an impact. Rhesus monkeys can be used effectively in studies of the musculoskeletal system in microgravity, as their physiology is similar to humans, and monkey experiments can be performed under controlled conditions to exclude the masking effect of countermeasures used by human subjects. This experiment examined the effect of microgravity and diminished motor activity (restraint) on the structure and metabolism of the m. vastus lateralis and m. soleus muscles of the Rhesus monkey.

fields.results: In the m. vastus lateralis postflight, both monkeys showed a significant decrease in the CSA of type I fibers. One of the monkeys also showed a significant decrease in the CSA of type II fibers. In R+17 capsule controls, significant decrease in the CSA of type I fibers was seen in only one monkey, and no change was seen in the CSA of type II fibers. In the vivarium controls, CSA of both fiber types increased. Total protein content remained essentially unchanged in the three groups of monkeys. Maximum oxygen uptake was lower in the flight animals than in the controls. SDH activity in the flight and capsule controls was unchanged in type I fibers, and lower in type II fibers. SDH activity in the vivarium controls remained essentially unchanged. In the m. soleus, flight monkeys showed a significant decrease in the CSA of type I fibers. One of the monkeys also showed a significant decrease in the CSA of type II fibers. The R+17 control monkeys showed mixed effects. In vivarium controls, three monkeys showed an increase in the CSA of type I fibers and one monkey showed a decrease. The CSA of type II fibers diminished in all vivarium animals. Total protein in type I fibers decreased in both flight animals, and the CSA of type II fibers decreased in one flight animal. In the vivarium controls, total protein remained essentially unchanged. The number of capillaries per fiber decreased in the m. soleus of both flight monkeys, but the capillary density varied differentially. The muscle atrophy observed in this experiment agrees with earlier studies on monkeys, rats, and humans.
fields.title: Structural and Metabolic Plasticity of Leg Muscle

fields.approach: Muscle biopsies were taken from the soleus (Sol), medial gastrocnemius (MG), tibialis anterior (TA), and vastus lateralis (VL), before and after a 14 day space flight. Samples were used to determine myosin heavy chain (MHC) composition, fiber type distribution, and fiber size. Single fibers from the soleus muscle were analyzed for cross-sectional area (CSA), myonuclear number/mm and myonuclear domain.

components.description: The Head Electronics Assembly (HEA) preconditioned signals from the sensors and provided signal pass through or preamplification for EOG, VNR, EEG, and brain temperature measurements. The HEA consisted of the mother board, which provided preamplification of EEG, EOG, and VNR signals,  and multiplexing of VNR signals; the daughter board, which provided a connection point for implanted sensors; and the baby board, which provided a connection point for ground based testing. fields.objectives: Although past experiments have proven that some muscles weaken and atrophy during space flight, the exact mechanism behind this is unknown. Three hypotheses help explain the phenomenon: 1) Some "normal" level of activity, which is lacking in microgravity, is needed to maintain normal muscle properties, 2) Force generated by a muscle is directly related to muscle fiber size, loss of which occurs in space, and 3) Hormonal deficiencies, such as those seen during microgravity exposure, contribute to a loss in muscle mass. This experiment will help to quantify the response of muscle to space flight.

payloads.description:
Mission Overview

Bion 11 was the payload that flew on the Cosmos biosatellite mission of 1996. The payload was a collaborative endeavor pursued by the American, Russian, and French space agencies. Its 14-day mission began on December 24, 1996 with the launch of the Vostok space capsule from the Plesetsk cosmodrome in Russia. The capsule carried two rhesus monkeys as well as other life sciences and microgravity experiments.

Bion 11 was intended to define qualitatively and quantitatively the effect of weightlessness on primate physiology and the mechanisms underlying those changes. Fields of investigation included the effects of weightlessness on bone, muscle and neuromuscular structure and function; sensorimotor function; behavior; circadian rhythms; fluid and electrolyte balance; and immunology.  Also studied was the way that the body readapts to normal gravity following landing.

Other Bion 11 experiments included a study of how a number of different organisms  respond physiologically to microgravity, including Dileptus anfer (a protist) Pottia and Caretodou mosses on agar, Lepidium savita L. seedlings on a solid substrate, fruit flies, black body beetles, and Spanish newts. Radiation experiments on dry seeds, nucleotides and bacterial spores were also conducted.

The Bion 11 flight was successfully completed when the spacecraft landed in Kazakhstan on January 7, 1997. One of the monkeys died during anesthesia induction for its post-landing medical operation and check-up, which occurred shortly after its capsule was recovered. This incident raised questions with respect to the use of anesthesia on astronauts post flight, and results of the investigation potentially saved the lives of future astronauts.  The Bion 11 and 12 investigations were supposed to have been a two-mission series with major objectives aimed at understanding the source of muscle and bone weakening in space; however, the monkey's death compromised certain of these studies.

fields.results: Percentage of pure type I fibers was decreased in the Sol postflight, in both the flight and the flight simulation groups. The number of hybrid fibers increased in both groups, and the MHC composition changed in a similar direction. In the MG or TA, no consistent changes in MHC, fiber type composition, or size of type II fibers were observed. However, pure type I fibers were smaller postflight in both the MG and the TA. In the single soleus fibers, mean CSAs of type I MHC fibers were smaller postflight. Mean myonuclear number/mm was similar between pre- and post-flight in all groups, but the mean myonuclear domains of the type I MHC fibers were decreased postflight. The Sol, a slow antigravity muscle, was affected the most by the 14 day space flight.
fields.title: Adaptations of Motor Control in Response to Spaceflight

fields.approach: The DEXA method was used to measure BMD of the lumbar vertebrae and the tibial lower third. Measurements included a whole body scan (for body mineral content and BMD of different skeletal compartments), a lumbar spine scan, and a regional scan of both tibia bones. The speed of ultrasound propagation (SOS) was measured in eight zones of the tibia. Measurements were taken before and after flight in flight, ground control, and vivarium animals.

fields.objectives: Loss of bone mineral mass (bone mineral density - BMD) due to microgravity exposure occurs primarily in the lumbar vertebrae, the proximal segment of the femoral bone, and the pelvic bone. BMD loss tends to develop in areas with a large percentage of trabecular (spongy) bone. BMD has not been observed to decrease in the upper body, such as the skull, arms, and ribs. No direct correlation between BMD and bone strength has been observed. This has made it difficult to predict the level of osteopenia an individual will experience during space flight. This experiment will examine 1) whether exposure to microgravity causes changes in the mass and structure of trabecular and cortical bone, and 2) whether postflight changes in the skeletal bone status can be examined by measuring the ultrasound propagation speed.

fields.results: Age-related increase in BMD was delayed in the flight animals. No absolute BMD loss was seen in the tibia; however, age-related BMD increase was delayed to a greater extent in the metabolically active trabecular bone compared to cortical bone. SOS measured before and after flight changed only slightly, indicating that exposure to microgravity decreased age-related bone development. However, bone changes observed may also have been associated with housing and training patterns. Compared to similar human data, the BMD gradient in the Bion monkeys remained essentially unchanged.
fields.title: Bone and Lean Body Mass Changes Following Spaceflight

fields.approach: Four months prior to launch, flight animals were implanted with electrodes in order to monitor and record their electrocardiogram (EKG), electrogastrogram (EGG), and rheopneumogram (RPG). Physiological data were recorded during flight for a period of five minutes every two hours. EKG signals were interpolated and resampled at 20 Hz. Breathing depth was measured as an rheopneumogram amplitude (Arpg). R-R interval, BR, and Arpg means were calculated.

fields.objectives: The mechanisms that regulate the autonomic nervous system undergo a pattern of adaptations as they adjust to microgravity. Alterations in gastric myoelectric activity can be used to evaluate changes in vagal and sympathetic effects. Varying R-R intervals allow sympathetic effects and vagal variations to be estimated. The vagal control of the heart can also be evaluated by the respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA). This study focused on the adaptation of rhesus monkeys' autonomic nervous system to microgravity and its effect upon cardiac and gastric rhythms.

fields.results: During space flight, the vagal effects upon both the cardiac and respiratory function varied between the two animals. In animal #357, gastric myoelectric activity was enhanced, which may be associated with the cessation of juice intake on flight day (FD) eleven. Early in the flight, #357's RSA increased despite an increase in Arpg, which suggests significantly lower vagal effects on the heart.  #484 had a lower level of gastric myoelectric activity when compared to the rest of the flight. RSA levels rose through the flight and then dropped after landing. Further analysis of the results for animal #484 suggests that vagal effects on both the cardiac system and gastric functions were lower at the beginning of the flight. In summary, the vagal effects in #357 increased at the beginning of the flight and then decreased towards the end while #484's decreased through the duration of the flight. Further, the inhibition of vagal effects in animal #484 was accompanied by space motion sickness symptoms.
fields.title: Effect of Microgravity on Sympathetic and Parasympathetic Compartments of the Autonomic Nervous System

fields.approach: Animals were flown on the fourteen day Bion 11 mission and housed in the BIOS-Primate capsules. While on a light-dark cycle of 16 hours of light followed by 8 hours of dark, the animals were offered food twice a day and given performance tests four times a day. Brain temperature (Tbr), head skin temperature (Thd), ankle skin temperature (Tank), motor activity (MA), heart rate (HR), and ambient temperature within the capsule (Tamb) were all recorded at ten second intervals and stored in a digital memory unit.

fields.objectives: Organisms coordinate physiological processes through their circadian system. Circadian rhythms ensure that activities occur at the most favorable time. Human health and performance can be adversely affected when the rhythm is desynchronized. Research has shown that alterations in gravitational forces, such as the exposure to microgravity that astronauts undergo, can affect circadian rhythms. This study attempts to analyze the effects that exposure to microgravity has upon the circadian rhythms of different individuals.

fields.results: Analysis of the data supports the hypothesis that the gravitational environment affects circadian rhythms. The circadian rhythm of flight animals showed a significant phase delay when compared to the control animals. Tbr in the two flight monkeys, the best indicator of the circadian rhythm of the deep body temperature, showed a slower rise during the day than that of control animals. However, no free-running rhythms were detected, and each animal had an average period of about twenty-four hours. This suggests that the Zeitgebers mask the changes in circadian rhythm. This is also evidenced by the distinct peaks in Thd that correspond to meals and performance tests. The increase in the endogenous period that remains within the entrainment range is the most probable mechanism by which the circadian rhythm does not transform into a free-running one.
fields.title: Circadian Rhythms of Macaca Mulatta During Spaceflight

Ambient temperature in the capsule was also measured at 10 second intervals. Flown monkeys (with the exception of #357) were used for post-flight control studies at R+17 and R+45.

fields.objectives: Non-thermal effects of microgravity on the body, such as gravitational and postural unloading of skeletal muscles, changes in muscle structure and function, headward blood shift, and changes in fluid and electrolyte homeostasis, may themselves cause thermal changes in the body. These thermal effects, such as changes in heat production, transfer, and release, may cause variations in body temperature and thermoregulatory disorders. This experiment examined the effects of microgravity on deep body temperature and skin temperature.

payloads.description:
Mission Overview

Bion 11 was the payload that flew on the Cosmos biosatellite mission of 1996. The payload was a collaborative endeavor pursued by the American, Russian, and French space agencies. Its 14-day mission began on December 24, 1996 with the launch of the Vostok space capsule from the Plesetsk cosmodrome in Russia. The capsule carried two rhesus monkeys as well as other life sciences and microgravity experiments.

Bion 11 was intended to define qualitatively and quantitatively the effect of weightlessness on primate physiology and the mechanisms underlying those changes. Fields of investigation included the effects of weightlessness on bone, muscle and neuromuscular structure and function; sensorimotor function; behavior; circadian rhythms; fluid and electrolyte balance; and immunology.  Also studied was the way that the body readapts to normal gravity following landing.

Other Bion 11 experiments included a study of how a number of different organisms  respond physiologically to microgravity, including Dileptus anfer (a protist) Pottia and Caretodou mosses on agar, Lepidium savita L. seedlings on a solid substrate, fruit flies, black body beetles, and Spanish newts. Radiation experiments on dry seeds, nucleotides and bacterial spores were also conducted.

The Bion 11 flight was successfully completed when the spacecraft landed in Kazakhstan on January 7, 1997. One of the monkeys died during anesthesia induction for its post-landing medical operation and check-up, which occurred shortly after its capsule was recovered. This incident raised questions with respect to the use of anesthesia on astronauts post flight, and results of the investigation potentially saved the lives of future astronauts.  The Bion 11 and 12 investigations were supposed to have been a two-mission series with major objectives aimed at understanding the source of muscle and bone weakening in space; however, the monkey's death compromised certain of these studies.

fields.results: Data were pooled across 6 Bion missions, using a total of 12 monkeys. In 8 out of 12 animals, a gradual decrease in mean deep body temperature (DBT) by 0.3-0.8 degrees Celsius was observed. DBT reached a minimum on flight days 4-8, then began to increase. Values of head temperature and leg temperature in space and on the ground were not significantly different. Out of the three skin temperatures measured, only ankle temperature (Tank) suggested that the skin region participates in physiologically controlled heat release; Tank usually varied inversely to DBT. An unusually high Tank increase versus DBT was seen at night during space flight; this may be due to blood redistribution in microgravity. Overall, the pooled data shows that the system of thermal regulation is adequate to support the normal range of DBT, even during high ambient temperatures.
fields.title: Thermoregulation in Macaca Mulatta during Spaceflight

fields.approach: Prior to the flight, male Sprague Dawley rats were anesthetized and subjected to bilateral adrenalectomy.  Pellets made of cholesterol with dissolved corticosterone and aldosterone were implanted in each adrenalectomized rat.  All rats had been injected with a label to mark the bone forming surfaces.  After the flight, serum samples of corticosterone and aldosterone concentrations were measured by radioimmunoassay techniques.  The left tibia was frozen and subsequently used to measure dry and ash bone weights.  Bone samples were sectioned, stained, and counterstained for measurements of cancellous bone volume  (%), osteoclast surface  (%), an index of cancellous bone resorption, and osteoblast surface (%), an index of cancellous bone formation.  The right tibia underwent a polymerization process and was cut into cross-sections.  From the cross-sections, cortical bone area, cortical width, and marrow area were measured.

hardware.description:
The Ambient Temperature Recorder (ATR-4) is a self-contained, battery-powered instrument, approximately the size of a deck of cards. It may be placed in almost any environment (not submersible in liquid) to provide recording of up to four channels of temperature data. Channel 1 is selectable for either internal or external probe temperature sensing. Channels 2 through 4 are external only and require individual external temperature probes. External probes are flexible to allow the user to place probes at various locations within the sensed environment. Standard length for probes is three feet, but they may be longer or shorter, if required.

The temperature range is -40 °C to +60 °C. Data sample rate and number of channels are user-selectable. The total number of samples (32,400) is limited by the size of the ATR-4's solid state memory. When the memory is full, the recorder stops recording. Stored data may be read out postflight using a serial interface unit and an IBM-compatible computer. Power for the ATR-4 is provided by two internal batteries. An O-ring seal protects the ATR-4's internal electronics from fluids in the environment and permits operation in damp or humid environments such as an animal habitat.

fields.objectives:
Data originated from Thomas Wronski's NASA grant "Role of Corticosteroids in Bone Loss During Space Flight."

Previous studies have shown that stress-induced corticosteroid hormones increase during spaceflight.  Negative effects on bone, such as decreased bone formation, are also associated with these hormones. The objective of this study was to determine whether corticosteroid excesses contribute to the bone loss that occur during spaceflight.

payloads.description:
NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center was responsible for the overall LMS mission management and for the microgravity investigations; the life sciences investigations were managed at the Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas. Four other space agencies joined NASA to support this mission: the Canadian Space Agency (CSA), Italian Space Agency (ASI), French Space Agency (CNES), and European Space Agency (ESA). Each of the space agencies contributed hardware and supported different experiments. 

Thirteen experiments conducted during the Life and Microgravity Spacelab mission were sponsored by US research institutes.  This research included studies in the field of neurovestibular adjustment, pulmonary function, physiology of muscles and bones, energy metabolism during space flight in humans and the effects of space flight on human performance, sleep and biological (circadian) rhythms. The biology investigations included studies on the development of the neural system in fish eggs, alterations in the metabolism of bone in rats and changes in the cell structure of conifer seedlings. 

The research performed during the LMS mission has the potential to significantly enhance the quality of life on Earth. If the structure of certain proteins can be determined with the help of the space-grown crystals, advances can be made to improve the treatment of many human diseases. Space investigations in physiological processes may lead to remedies for loss of bone or muscle mass suffered by astronauts and people on Earth with osteoporosis. Electronic materials research in space may help refine manufacturing processes on Earth, leading to improved products, like computers, lasers and other high-tech devices. Using the unique environment of space to conduct science investigations in biology and physics increases scientists' understanding of these fundamental processes.

fields.results: From the data in this study, it was found that rats in both the experiment and control populations had increased in body weight.  This result indicated that the rats went through the flight well and were healthy.  The flight group that did not undergo adrenalectomy showed significant increased adrenal gland weights.  Thus, it suggests that the rats had corticosteroid excess during spaceflight.  It was determined that the intact flight rats had normal bone mass, thus the objective of this experiment was not met.

fields.approach: Animals were injected with a dose of ketamine at 5 mg/kg of body weight before flight, several hours after landing, and during the readaptation period. Five minutes after injection, blood was drawn and the serum prepared. Using both the Wet-Test biochemical analyzer and dry slides, albumin, BUN, creatine, globulin, alkaline phosphatase, alanine aminotransferase, glutamate, dehydrogenase, calcium, phosphate, and bilirubin were measured.

fields.objectives: Previous research has shown that exposure to microgravity leads to changes in both human and animals' metabolisms. Some effects include a new homeostasis and alterations in energy, carbohydrate, lipid, fluid-electrolyte, and protein metabolism. This study investigates the metabolism of rhesus monkeys before, during, and after a fourteen day space flight.

fields.results: The flight animals had a biochemical baseline within normal limits of similarly aged rhesus monkeys. At landing, total protein, BUN, albumin, and calcium content had changed significantly. Phosphate concentration was at the baseline level. Alkaline phosphatase, glutamate, alanine aminotransferase, dehydrogenase, creatine and bilirubin levels were unaltered at landing and remained the same during readaptation. From this, it can be concluded that the capsule was sufficient to comfortably support the animals for the fourteen day mission. Alterations in calcium level suggest that calcium usage changes in microgravity. Further analysis leads to the conclusion that carbohydrate metabolism was not altered significantly during flight.
fields.title: Energy Metabolism of Macaca Mulatta During Space Flight

fields.approach: Soleus and gastrocnemius muscles of the flight and control animals were biopsied approximately four months preflight. Flight animals were biopsied one and two days postflight. Two flight simulation controls were biopsied after 14 days restraint. Small cross-sections were cut from the bottom of the samples and used for determination of myofibrillar and mitochondrial density. The remaining portions were divided longitudinally into three sections, skinned, and separated into single fibers. Single fibers were used to measure peak force (P0), the force-velocity relationship, the pCa-force relationship, maximal unloaded shortening velocity (V0), and peak rate of tension redevelopment (ktr). Fibers were then solubilized and used to determine the myosin heavy and light chain isozyme profiles. Remaining single fibers were freeze-dried and assayed for biochemical content by enzymatic cycling.

fields.objectives: A rapid decline in the mass and force of rat hind limb extensor muscles has been shown to result from weightlessness. A reduction in peak power has also been observed in the rat soleus muscle despite an increased maximal shortening velocity. In humans, declines in voluntary peak isometric ankle extensor torque have been observed following both long- and short-term space flight. A more complete understanding of how the physiological and biochemical processes of muscle function are altered during space flight is needed. In this experiment, investigators will attempt to determine the extent to which the isotonic contractile properties of the slow- and fast-twitch fiber types of the soleus and gastrocnemius muscles are altered by a 14-day space flight. Elevated velocity in the antigravity slow type I fibers, and the extent to which weightlessness alters glycolytic and oxidative enzyme capacity of individual slow- and fast-twitch fibers, were also examined.

fields.results: Growth had no significant effects on the diameter or peak force of slow type I fibers. In contrast, fiber diameter and peak force declined in both flight and flight simulation animals. Relative force decreased only in flight animals. A larger flight-induced decline in fiber size and peak force was observed in the gastrocnemius than the soleus, but could be explained by muscle atrophy alone, as relative force stayed the same. Post-flight, type II fibers in the gastrocnemius showed a 28% decline in relative force, but no significant change in fiber diameter or peak force. Maximal shortening velocity increased during weightlessness, which could be explained by growth. Postflight, soleus type I fibers showed a shifted pCa-force relationship. However, changes in Ca2+ sensitivity were attributed to growth, as the growth controls showed the same effects. Myofibrillar volume density of the soleus fibers was unchanged by flight. No significant effect of space flight was seen on any of the glycolytic enzymes, in either the slow- or fast-twitch fiber types. The primary effects of space flight were type I fiber atrophy and reduced peak force and power.
fields.title: Effect of Weightlessness on Single Muscle Fiber Function in Rhesus Monkeys

fields.approach: Biopsies were taken from the distal MTJ region in the soleus muscles of flight and vivarium control monkeys after the 14-day space flight. Since the MTJ morphology would not significantly differ after a 14-day period, no growth control biopsies were used. Biopsies were fixed in a graded series of glutaraldehyde solution in 0.4 M cacodylate buffer at pH 7.4, then postfixed in a 2% osmium tetroxide solution. The fixed samples were dehydrated, then embedded in epoxy resin and cut into longitudinal ultra-thin sections (70 nm) through the muscle-tendon interface. The sections were mounted on copper grids and stained with uranyl and lead citrate for electron microscopy.

fields.objectives: Previous studies have shown that both space flight and simulated microgravity (hind limb suspension) induce ultrastructural changes in the myotendinous junction (MTJ) of the soleus in the rat. The MTJ is a specialized region of skeletal muscle fibers where the muscle-tendon interface is increased by folding of the muscle fiber plasma membrane. The increased surface area results in reduced stress to the plasma membrane during contraction. A chronic change in muscle use and/or loading leads to a structural remodeling of the MTJ. Previously, only one histological study has examined the muscle-tendon interface in non-human primates. This experiment will examine the effects of space flight on the soleus MTJ ultrastructure in the rhesus.

fields.results: Structural remodeling occurred at the MTJs after a 14-day space flight, in a similar manner as observed in rat soleus MTJs during the SLS-2 mission. Soleus MTJs of the flight monkeys appeared more shredded than vivarium control MTJs, due to deeper and larger invaginations of the plasma membrane. As observed in rats, the larger, deeper invaginations of the sarcolemma seemed to increase the myotendinous interface. Signs of membrane and basal lamina remodeling were also observed. Granular and vesicular globules observed at the MTJs are likely due to muscle fiber degenerative material. An alteration of contractile material and myofilament anchoring structures was suggested by the presence of numerous vacuoles and caveolae along the lateral sides of the muscle fiber processes. Unlike in the rat soleus MTJ, the contractile apparatus in the rhesus monkey appeared to be less affected by a 14-day space flight. The only misalignment observed was that of adjacent Z disks in the parajunctional region. The structural remodeling described appears to be influenced both by weightlessness and constrained movement during flight.
fields.title: Morphological and Functional Adaptations of Muscle Fibers Myo-tendonous Junction to Hypokinesia and Hypogravity

fields.approach: Two sets of muscle biopsies were performed on each group of monkeys: flight, 1G simulation control, and vivarium control (used to simulate growth effects). Biopsies were taken from the biceps and the deep portion of the triceps medialis. Baseline biopsies were taken approximately five months before in-flight (control) or postflight biopsies. Fibers were EGTA-skinned and examined for structural and functional properties. Single fiber types were analyzed by SDS-PAGE for their myosin heavy chain (MHC) composition, and identified as either slow, fast, slow hybrid, or fast hybrid. After being structurally identified, each fiber was studied for its functional Ca activation characteristics (T/pCa curves).

fields.objectives: Atrophy of some lower limb muscles, especially the antigravity muscles, has been observed in animals exposed to microgravity. Few studies have been done on the effects of microgravity on the upper limbs. Primates appear to be a good model for examining muscle contractile and biochemical properties, and making EMG recordings. This experiment will examine the effects of microgravity on the slow-type muscle of the triceps and the fast-type muscle of the biceps.

payloads.description:
Mission Overview

Bion 11 was the payload that flew on the Cosmos biosatellite mission of 1996. The payload was a collaborative endeavor pursued by the American, Russian, and French space agencies. Its 14-day mission began on December 24, 1996 with the launch of the Vostok space capsule from the Plesetsk cosmodrome in Russia. The capsule carried two rhesus monkeys as well as other life sciences and microgravity experiments.

Bion 11 was intended to define qualitatively and quantitatively the effect of weightlessness on primate physiology and the mechanisms underlying those changes. Fields of investigation included the effects of weightlessness on bone, muscle and neuromuscular structure and function; sensorimotor function; behavior; circadian rhythms; fluid and electrolyte balance; and immunology.  Also studied was the way that the body readapts to normal gravity following landing.

Other Bion 11 experiments included a study of how a number of different organisms  respond physiologically to microgravity, including Dileptus anfer (a protist) Pottia and Caretodou mosses on agar, Lepidium savita L. seedlings on a solid substrate, fruit flies, black body beetles, and Spanish newts. Radiation experiments on dry seeds, nucleotides and bacterial spores were also conducted.

The Bion 11 flight was successfully completed when the spacecraft landed in Kazakhstan on January 7, 1997. One of the monkeys died during anesthesia induction for its post-landing medical operation and check-up, which occurred shortly after its capsule was recovered. This incident raised questions with respect to the use of anesthesia on astronauts post flight, and results of the investigation potentially saved the lives of future astronauts.  The Bion 11 and 12 investigations were supposed to have been a two-mission series with major objectives aimed at understanding the source of muscle and bone weakening in space; however, the monkey's death compromised certain of these studies.
